newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian industrial giant plunges into red.
newsitem.headline: Australian industrial giant plunges into red.

text.p: Australian-based industrial group Pacific Dunlop Ltd dived into red ink in the latest year after booking a hefty abnormal loss to put two years of "sobering" financial woes behind it, it said on Friday.
Pacific Dunlop declared a net loss of A$132 million (US$105 million) for the year to June 30.

The figures included a large net abnormal loss of A$296 million, reflecting management's decision to cast off its troubled U.S. medical equipment unit and book over A$80 million in restructuring charges and asset writedowns.

"This is a clean-out result and it gives both myself and my managenent team an absolutely clean slate on which to write the next chapter of Pacific Dunlop's history," group managing director Rod Chadwick said.

Pacific Dunlop's recent history has been dominated by severe problems faced by its Telectronics subsidiary, which is now up for sale after a defect in one of its cardiac-implant products effectively put the unit out of business for 13 months.
"We have so far had six deaths from this problem over the last two years," chairman John Gough told reporters.
The problem was first detected in Telectronics Accufix pacemaker lead in late 1994.
Gough said the company was now in advanced negotiations for the sale of Telectronics, whose losses accounted for A$340 million of gross abnormal losses.

He declined to comment any further on the sale talks, but the news helped buoy Pacific Dunlop shares on the local stock market, where the share price closed up five cents at A$2.70 on Friday after touching an intraday high of A$2.73.
Gough, who presided over rapid expansion of the group in the 1980s, said Pacific Dunlop's remaining businesses were inherently strong and predicted a pick-up in earnings in 1996/97.
He conceded, however, that conglomerates were no longer fashionable.

"The day of building conglomerates is past," Gough said, reflecting on the 1995 sales of the group's food business and its Cochlear hearing-aid business, leaving Pacific Dunlop focused on batteries, tyres, cables, rubber gloves and condoms, clothing and distribution of car-parts.
Pacific Dunlop has operations in Australia, New Zealand, Asia and North America, and turned over A$6.5 billion in sales in 1995/96.

The company slashed its borrowing in 1995/96, announced a refocusing of the firm's businesses into three main groups, set a target to increase profit margins, and forecast a pick-up in pre-abnormal net earnings in 1996/97.
